findings: Single radiographic projection of an upper extremity showing the distal humerus, elbow joint, both forearm bones (radius and ulna), and the flexed hand/wrist. A transverse lucent line with mild cortical step-off is visible crossing the mid-diaphysis of the medially positioned forearm bone (consistent with the ulna), seen in the original image and confirmed on contrast-enhanced, sharpened, and edge-enhanced views as well as on magnified crops. Alignment across this line appears preserved without gross displacement or angulation on this single view. The adjacent forearm bone (radius) shows no visible cortical discontinuity. The elbow joint (distal humerus, olecranon, radial head) shows smooth, congruent articular surfaces without visible fracture, dislocation, or effusion. The hand is imaged in a flexed/clenched position, causing overlap of the phalanges and carpal bones on this projection; no definite fracture or dislocation is identified within the visualized hand and wrist, though overlap limits assessment of individual bones. No definite periosteal reaction or focal soft tissue swelling is confidently identified, though soft tissue detail is limited by image contrast/windowing.
impression: Findings are most consistent with a nondisplaced (or minimally displaced) transverse fracture of the mid-shaft of one forearm bone, most likely the ulna, based on this single view. The radius, elbow joint, and visualized hand/wrist bones appear grossly intact, though the flexed hand position limits full evaluation of the carpal bones and phalanges.
limitations: Only a single radiographic projection is provided; standard fracture evaluation requires at least two orthogonal views (e.g., AP and lateral) to confirm the fracture, exclude a second (both-bone) injury, and assess displacement, angulation, and rotation, none of which can be reliably determined from this image alone. The flexed/overlapping position of the fingers and carpal bones limits assessment of the hand and wrist for subtle fracture or dislocation. Image contrast and windowing limit soft tissue evaluation. This analysis is intended as a second-opinion support aid only and does not substitute for review by a qualified radiologist or clinician with full clinical context and complete imaging series.
